slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open by telling students that this chapter is not a parade of mistaken arguments. The historical attempts are useful because each one exposes a premise that felt visually obvious but was not licensed by neutral geometry. The lecture treats the span from printed pages 148 to 176 as a map of assumptions under stress.

slides.title: Chapter Route
slides.notes: Use this route slide to set the classroom contract. The lecture will not judge old arguments only by whether they proved the postulate. Instead, it asks what each argument needed in order to work. That shift is the bridge from history to foundations and prepares students for the independence viewpoint in the next chapter.

slides.title: The Axiom Under Pressure
slides.notes: Point out that the drawing deliberately contains more candidate directions than the Euclidean conclusion will permit. The mathematical pressure is not the existence of a line through the point, but the global claim about meeting or not meeting a given line. This prepares students to distrust visual obviousness without distrusting diagrams altogether.

slides.title: Failed Proof Trace
slides.notes: This is the method slide for the whole lecture. Ask students to separate an argument into construction lines and inference lines before they decide whether it is convincing. In the historical material, many errors are not bad drawings but unmarked inferences. The dependency trace makes the unmarked inference visible enough to discuss.

slides.title: Proclus
slides.notes: Present Proclus as an example of a very reasonable visual instinct that is still too strong for neutral geometry. Equal distance feels natural when two drawn lines look parallel, but the argument needs more than the picture supplies. The useful lesson is that metric language can carry a parallel assumption even when no formal parallel axiom is named.

slides.title: Wallis
slides.notes: Use Wallis to show how algebraic or transformational habits can arrive earlier than the axioms allow. Similarity is familiar to students, so it may look too mild to question. The key point is that a same-shape copy at a new size is precisely the sort of behavior that neutral geometry cannot simply assume.

slides.title: Saccheri
slides.notes: This slide is the first major geometric lab in the lecture. Saccheri's quadrilateral organizes the problem into summit-angle regimes, which is more precise than arguing from a freehand picture. Tell students to read the three panels as branches in a proof search: each branch must be eliminated by licensed reasoning, not by visual preference.

slides.title: Lambert
slides.notes: Lambert's contribution is useful here because it converts a proof branch into a geometric diagnostic. The fourth angle is not merely a local measurement; it hints at the curvature behavior of the surrounding geometry. Stress that this is still pre-model intuition, so the slide should be read as a gauge rather than a finished consistency proof.

slides.title: Legendre
slides.notes: Legendre's angle-sum strategy gives students a compact diagnostic they can carry forward. The instructor should emphasize that the bar chart is not pretending to prove the cases. It shows why angle sum becomes a useful observable: a small triangle statement can reflect the larger parallel structure once the correct assumptions are in place.

slides.title: Hidden Assumption Ledger
slides.notes: Treat the ledger as a reusable checklist for later chapters. It lets students see that the historical narrative has been converted into mathematical warnings: metric persistence, similarity, branch elimination, curvature interpretation, and angle-sum inference. Those warnings are valuable because they tell a reader exactly where a proof should slow down.

slides.title: Neutral Workbench
slides.notes: This slide names the discipline that keeps the historical chapter from becoming vague. Diagrams, models, computations, and proofs all matter, but each layer has a different job. Ask students to identify which layer is speaking whenever an argument feels persuasive. Most hidden assumptions occur when one layer quietly borrows authority from another.

slides.title: Timeline Map
slides.notes: Use the map to shift from local examples back to chapter structure. The important point is not that every historical detail is represented, but that each named attempt supplies a different kind of pressure. The directed arrows say that the mathematical problem is being transformed, not simply repeated by different authors.

slides.title: Regime Lab
slides.notes: Frame the regime lab as an operational version of the historical story. The diagram makes it possible to talk about branches without pretending that the branch picture is itself a proof. Students should learn to ask which assumption moves the argument from possible cases to a single outcome. That question is the real lab result.

slides.title: Evidence Types
slides.notes: This slide makes the epistemic distinction explicit. Historical attempts often failed because one kind of evidence was treated as if it answered a stronger question. A diagram may be excellent evidence for what to investigate, and a model may be excellent evidence for consistency or failure, but neither removes the need to name the proof assumptions.

slides.title: Proof Audit Exercise
slides.notes: This is an instructor-ready activity, but keep it deliberately unfinished. The goal is not to give students a polished counterargument on the slide. The goal is to train an audit habit: locate the first line whose authority is unclear. That habit carries directly into reading Saccheri, Lambert, and later model-based independence arguments.

slides.title: Bridge to Independence
slides.notes: Use this bridge to prepare the next chapter without racing ahead. The historical attempts matter because they give names and locations to assumptions. Once an assumption is explicit, model building can test whether changing it destroys the system or produces a new geometry. That is the conceptual doorway to hyperbolic geometry.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close by returning to the chapter's central transformation. Historical attempts did not merely fail; they helped mathematicians learn how to read an argument for hidden Euclidean content. The class should leave with a practical method: diagram the proof, name the imported assumption, and ask how a model would behave if that assumption changed.
